newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sterling slide relieves pressure on Irish pound.
newsitem.headline: Sterling slide relieves pressure on Irish pound.

text.p: A three-pfennig fall in sterling following Labour's landslide victory in the British election coupled with a half-percentage point rise in Irish interest rates relieved pressure on a battered Irish pound on Friday, dealers said.
"Sterling's fall certainly has alleviated some of the pressure. If sterling stays around these levels or weakens further, it solves a lot of problems for the Irish pound," one dealer said.

The punt has come under heavy pressure in recent days as speculators sold the currency, believing it would have to fall closer to its central rate in the ERM if Ireland is to join European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The punt shed four percent against the mark on Wednesday and Thursday and plunged over three percent against sterling, hitting a five-year low against the British currency.
But it clambered back above 0.9300 sterling in early trade on Friday and firmed to over 2.5800 marks, helped by sterling weakness in the election aftermath.
Sterling shed around three pfennigs in early trade as dealers took profits and trimmed long positions in the wake of the Labour Party's sweeping victory in the British elections.
Analysts said there was also some concern in the market about the size of Labour's likely parliamentary majority.

"A more moderate majority of 60 or 70 seats would have been taken quite well by the markets but Labour is seen to have been given an untethered hand with what they can or cannot do," Pat O'Sullivan, economist at AIB Capital Markets told Reuters.
Sterling/mark was trading at 2.7690 marks by 0930 GMT after trading close to 2.8000 yesterday.

This allowed the Irish pound to firm to 0.9340 sterling from 0.9180 at Thursday's close. Against the mark, the punt dipped to 2.5590 this morning before recovering to 2.5860 marks from 2.5616 last night.
Analysts said the Irish pound was also helped by a half-point rise in official Irish interest rates late yesterday.
The Central Bank surprised the market when it announced that it was raising the official short-term facility rate to 6.75 percent from 6.25 percent with effect from May 2.
Analysts believe the sharp and sudden drop in the value of the Irish pound, particularly on a trade-weighted basis, fuelled fears of inflation at the bank, triggering the rate increase.

"The central bank will be very unhappy with the way the currency is on a trade-weighted basis in particular. If you go back to their monetary policy statement back in February, they did say if the currency fell on a trade-weighted basis, rates would have to go higher," Oliver Mangan, bond economist at AIB Capital Markets, told Reuters.
While the rise was seen as unlikely to please the government, which is widely expected to call an election for June 6, it helped bolster the punt to some extent.

"The rate rise had an effect. It made it more expensive for overseas investors to sell the Irish pound and took some of the pressure off the currency but the key feature this morning is the weakening of sterling. That has eased the pressure considerably," AIB's O'Sullivan said.
